title: CypressEdge - Private connectivity & VPC options discovery
summary: Intro discovery to map networking constraints for a private Redwood deployment. Customer needs cross-account VPC peering or PrivateLink, non-overlapping CIDRs, egress controls, KMS integration, and region placement for EU data residency. Agreed to share diagrams, a Terraform peering example, and schedule a technical deep-dive next week.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-17 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Avery Chen, Miguel Ramos (Redwood); Dana Liu, Harold Kim, Sofia Torres (CypressEdge)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on private deployment network topology, security reqs, and next steps. Transcript quality: medium; occasional mis-transcription.

[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Avery, AE on the account; Miguel is our solutions engineer. Dana, Harold, Sofia, thanks for the time — do you want to do quick intros?

[00:12] Dana Liu: Hi all, I'm Dana, CTO at CypressEdge. We're a data analytics platform, heavily regulated EU customers. I'll lead architecture decisions.

[00:19] Harold Kim: Harold, infrastructure. I run the cloud networking team. Today we want to figure out how Redwood would sit in our VPC estate and what connectivity patterns you support.

[00:28] Sofia Torres: Sofia, security. Focus on encryption, key management, audit trails, and SSO integration.

[00:34] Miguel Ramos: Great. My role is to map the technical constraints and propose config patterns. We'll ask about current infra, CIDR space, transit gateway usage, and compliance needs.

[01:05] Dana Liu: To frame, we need a private deployment inside our AWS account or peering to a Redwood-managed VPC. We cannot have any public internet egress for model payloads — all must be inside EU regions.

[01:18] Avery Chen: Understood. Two primary options: private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink / Azure Private Link) or VPC peering. Each has tradeoffs on routing and cross-account management. Curious — are you leaning towards hosting the control plane in your account fully (private deployment) or peering to Redwood-hosted nodes?

[01:37] Harold Kim: Ideally we host the runtime inside our AWS account for auditability — but there may be cost implications. If we peer to Redwood's dedicated VPC, we need strong isolation and full flow logs. The question is what Redwood supports out of the box.

[01:56] Miguel Ramos: We support both patterns. For Private deployments we can ship a customer-controlled control plane or run a private control plane in your VPC depending on the contract. For hosted-but-private connectivity we commonly use PrivateLink for management/control and VPC peering for data plane where low latency is required.

[02:16] Sofia Torres: On encryption/KMS: keys must be customer-managed via KMS and all model logs must be available. Do you integrate with customer KMS/HSMs?

[02:25] Miguel Ramos: Yes, we have KMS integrations for both hosted and private; for on-prem or VPC customers we can plug into your CMKs. HSM integrations need a contractual addendum but technically supported. We'll share our security checklist.

[02:41] Dana Liu: About IP addressing — we have a limited CIDR range. Overlapping CIDRs are a dealbreaker. How do you handle CIDR conflicts if Redwood-managed VPCs clash with ours?

[02:51] Miguel Ramos: We require non-overlapping ranges for peering. If you want Redwood-managed VPC peering, we'd request a /16 or /20 block range in your VPC mapping doc. For PrivateLink the route is via ENIs and you don't need global non-overlap for service endpoints, but DNS may get trickier.

[03:13] Harold Kim: Transit Gateway is a factor — we route many accounts through a central TGW. Would Redwood peering terminate at our TGW?

[03:21] Avery Chen: We have customers terminate peering to their TGW; that adds flexibility. We need to validate route propagation and security groups. Sometimes TGW route tables block AWS PrivateLink endpoints by policy, so that's something to test.

[03:42] Sofia Torres: DNS resolution for private endpoints — we need internal FQDNs, split-horizon DNS, and cert verification. Will Redwood publish private zone names we can resolve internally?

[03:51] Miguel Ramos: Yes, for PrivateLink we provide a private DNS option that you can authorize in your account. For peering we'd rely on your internal DNS or conditional forwarding. There can be delays if your DNS doesn't forward properly, which causes a lot of tickets.

[04:12] Dana Liu: Region constraints: our data residency mandate requires all inference to happen in eu-west-1, and logs kept within EU. Does Redwood allow pinning model serving to a single region and avoiding cross-region fallbacks?

[04:24] Miguel Ramos: Absolutely. We can pin model serving to a single region and disable cross-region fallbacks in the routing policy. For hosted customers we offer region controls; for private deployment it's typically guaranteed by where you run the runtime.

[04:40] Harold Kim: Latency is critical — we're doing synchronous inference at 90ms p95. If we peer over inter-region connections, does Redwood support colocating runtime in our AZs?

[04:52] Avery Chen: We can pin to AZs and even specific instance types if you go Dedicated or Private. With inter-region traffic you'll get additional latency; best path is same-region peering or colocated runtime.

[05:08] Dana Liu: Auditing and logs: we require immutable audit logs for token use and request traces for 12 months. Do you export flow logs and per-request traces to customer S3 or SIEM?

[05:19] Miguel Ramos: Yes, we can forward audit logs to your S3 or SIEM via Kinesis/CloudWatch exports. We keep internal telemetry but push a copy to your account for retention; we'll need an agreed schema to map request IDs.

[05:34] Sofia Torres: SSO and RBAC — we need SCIM/SAML and fine-grained roles for who can create model endpoints. Any limits there?

[05:44] Miguel Ramos: SCIM + SAML are supported; we can map roles to your IAM constructs or manage role sync from the console. For private deployments you'll likely integrate with your internal IDP.

[05:58] Harold Kim: Back to connectivity: what's the egress model? If runtime pulls base models from our S3, do you require internet egress for model downloads or can that be done within the VPC?

[06:10] Miguel Ramos: Model artifacts can be pulled from S3 via VPC endpoints (no internet egress). For initial provisioning we have nm — sorry, some bootstrap calls to our control plane; for fully isolated on-prem we have an air-gap workflow but it requires a special package.

[06:28] Dana Liu: What's the recommended pattern for cross-account peering? We operate a multi-account org and prefer not to open broad peering.

[06:36] Avery Chen: Typical is peering per account with least-privilege route tables. Another pattern is to terminate Redwood peering to a central networking account behind TGW and then use prefix lists and route controls. We'll send our Terraform patterns.

[06:51] Harold Kim: Security groups — do you expect us to open large ranges to allow traffic to the Redwood infra? We want tight security group rules.

[06:59] Miguel Ramos: We provide a minimal port list (usually 443 for control plane, and specific ports for data plane TLS endpoints). We can support mutual TLS for service-to-service and restrict by security group or prefix list.

[07:15] Sofia Torres: Can you confirm whether flow logs will include full request metadata or just network-level info?

[07:22] Miguel Ramos: Flow logs are network-level (accept/reject, src/dst/bytes). For per-request telemetry we push structured logs with request IDs, latency, model name, token counts — those are application-level and we can ship to your SIEM.

[07:40] Dana Liu: We need sample configs — route tables, security group examples, TF modules.

[07:45] Miguel Ramos: We'll provide a Terraform module for peering + PrivateLink and an example of TGW termination. I'll attach a sample routing table and an IP planning worksheet.

[08:02] Avery Chen: Quick note on rollback and service continuity — if your TGW blocks routes or there is CIDR overlap, what happens? We typically fail closed and switch to a canary fallback, but if you've blocked connectivity the control plane can't manage the runtime. We recommend a read-only fallback.

[08:22] Harold Kim: About SLA and support hours — we need 24x5 support for production traffic and a runbook for incident handling. Is that part of Dedicated/Private contracts?

[08:32] Avery Chen: Yes, Dedicated and Private come with enterprise support tiers. We provide runbooks, on-call contacts, and can set up playbooks with your SRE team.

[08:44] Sofia Torres: Legal question: data ingress vs egress classification. If we peer to a Redwood-managed VPC in EU, but control plane components sit in another region, does that count as cross-border data flow?

[08:56] Miguel Ramos: It depends on what metadata is sent to the control plane. We can configure the control plane to be within EU for regulated customers or arrange that metadata is routed to your EU control plane. We'll escalate to legal to produce a clear data flow diagram.

[09:15] Dana Liu: Demo/status: we want a proof-of-concept for a small steady traffic pattern; 10 qps at 128-token average. Scope would be 2–4 weeks. What do you need to run that in our account?

[09:29] Miguel Ramos: For a POC we need an IAM role, VPC peering setup or PrivateLink, KMS access to decrypt model artifacts (if used), and a small dedicated pool of GPUs or shared infra pinned to your region. We'll prepare a POC checklist.

[09:50] Harold Kim: Cost — private options vs hosted. Give us ballpark pricing for a Dedicated pool vs peering to Redwood-hosted nodes.

[10:00] Avery Chen: We'll send an estimated pricing sheet. High level: Dedicated reserved capacity is higher fixed cost but predictable; peering to hosted is lower fixed but has per-token/instance variable. We'll include egress network pricing if cross-region.

[10:18] Sofia Torres: Compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001, and penetration test reports?

[10:25] Miguel Ramos: We can share our SOC 2 report and penetration test summary under an NDA. For Private deployments we can accommodate audits and co-locate logs in your logging account.

[10:40] Dana Liu: A few nitty-gritty items: 1) we require no outbound to public internet from runtime; 2) route tables must be explicit; 3) we need proof the KMS keys never leave the EU.

[10:54] Miguel Ramos: Noted. For (1) we will document VPC endpoint options; for (2) sample route tables; for (3) we'll confirm key residency and KMS key policy.

[11:07] Harold Kim: Anything around throughput shaping? We might want to throttle or shape to protect backend services.

[11:14] Miguel Ramos: We have per-tenant throttles and rate-limits you can configure by route. Also burst controls at the runtime level.

[11:26] Dana Liu: Could we see a reference architecture for TGW + peering + PrivateLink hybrid? Many of our accounts need both patterns.

[11:33] Avery Chen: Yes, will send a hybrid pattern doc showing where PrivateLink is better (control plane) and where peering is for low-latency data. We'll include diagrams for 1) single-account runtime, 2) TGW-terminated peering, 3) PrivateLink-managed control plane.

[11:50] Sofia Torres: For the POC, we need a security review pack and the list of required IAM permissions.

[11:57] Miguel Ramos: We'll include an IAM least-privilege policy, required CloudWatch/Kinesis roles, and S3 bucket policies for logs.

[12:10] Dana Liu: Any blockers you foresee?

[12:14] Miguel Ramos: The main blockers are CIDR overlap and TGW policy restrictions. If those are resolved quickly we can get a POC environment stood up in under a week. For air-gapped on-prem it's a longer path.

[12:26] Avery Chen: Recap and next steps — we'll 1) send network diagram templates and Terraform module, 2) send security and SOC2 docs under NDA, 3) provide POC checklist and pricing, 4) schedule a deeper technical session to walk through TGW routing next Tuesday.

[12:45] Dana Liu: Works for us. Thanks.

[12:48] Harold Kim: I'll circulate our CIDR worksheet and TGW route table dump.

[12:52] Sofia Torres: I'll follow up with a list of compliance questions to prioritize.

[12:56] Avery Chen: Great, we'll follow up within two business days with the artifacts. Thanks everyone.

[13:05] (call ends)

Notes about transcript: occasional words garbled (e.g., "nm" or "sigh-der" for CIDR). Speakers occasionally overlap; speaker labels auto-attributed by system.
